Revised 2026-10-12 after the second-analyst review in `REVIEW.md`; the
point-by-point response is in `RESPONSE-TO-REVIEW.md`.

## The ask

Do the IRS data show any patterns in nonprofit locations and finances for
Nashville, alongside recent survey work on the Tennessee nonprofit workforce
(see `docs/`)? Exploratory only, five hours, no committed product.
Requester specifics are in the gitignored `_private.md`.

## Geography

Two units are reported throughout.

- **Davidson County** is Metro Nashville. Nashville has a consolidated
  city-county government, so the county is the city. Six small satellite
  cities inside the county (Goodlettsville, Belle Meade, Berry Hill, Forest
  Hills, Oak Hill, Ridgetop) are included.
- **The metro** is OMB CBSA 34980, Nashville-Davidson--Murfreesboro--Franklin,
  TN: Davidson plus 13 collar counties (Williamson, Rutherford, Sumner,
  Wilson, Maury, Robertson, Dickson, Cheatham, Hickman, Macon, Smith, Cannon,
  Trousdale), 2023 delineation, held fixed across years.

Geography is composed by joining the published `county-fips` and `cbsa`
crosswalks onto the geocoded Unified BMF. Location is the organization's
**current** filing address as carried in the BMF, applied to every year of
its history. Organizations headquartered in Davidson (Second Harvest, United
Way, the community action agencies) serve the region, so any per-resident
figure by county overstates how concentrated services are, and nothing in
these data constrains how far a Davidson organization's services reach.

**Benchmarks.** Nineteen peer metros chosen by the analyst (Memphis,
Knoxville, Austin, Charlotte, Raleigh, Indianapolis, Louisville, Columbus,
Kansas City, Jacksonville, Oklahoma City, Atlanta, Denver, St. Louis,
Cincinnati, Richmond, Birmingham, San Antonio, Phoenix). They are not the
Tennessee Nonprofit Network peer states used in the survey brief. The metro
is compared with whole peer metros. Davidson is compared with one county per
peer metro, the county with the most registered organizations. That is a
convenience, not a definition of the central city: it picks St. Louis County
rather than St. Louis city and Henrico rather than Richmond city. Rankings
"of 20" are rankings among these 20 counties or 20 metros. "Rest of US"
always means organizations outside the 20 metros and outside Tennessee;
"Peer metros" means the 19 others combined.

## Data

| Source | What it gives | Years | Currency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geocoded Unified BMF (vintage 2026_09, sha256 in `_pins.csv`) | Every registered organization: current address and classification, ruling date, first and last vintage observed, latest reported revenue and assets | 1989-2026 | Monthly; current |
| E-file v2.1 Form 990 Part I and Part IX (legacy NODC release, slated for supersession) | Employees, volunteers, revenue, expenses, net assets, compensation lines | TY2012-2023 | Lags two to three years |
| NCCS e-file Phase 0 `government_grants` (v2026.06, sha256 verified) | Form 990 Part VIII line 1e | TY2020-2023 | Lags two to three years |
| Census county population estimates (vintages 2019, 2023) | Denominators | 2010-2023 | |
| BLS QCEW annual county files | Private-sector average annual pay per job, Davidson | 2019, 2023 | |

**Main population for the financial and workforce tables:** organizations
with current BMF subsection 501(c)(3) that filed the full Form 990,
excluding hospitals and universities (NTEE v2 subsectors HOS and UNI).
Form 990-PF filers are absent because only return type 990 is read. Two
Nashville filers carry a private-foundation code in the current BMF
(Gibson Foundation, Dr Lynn Hicks Foundation); they are kept and noted.
Rows without a BMF match (about 1% of full-990 returns) are dropped.

**Filing selection.** One filing per EIN and tax year, chosen on Part I by
latest return timestamp with the filing identifier as tie-break; Part IX is
joined on the filing identifier, so both parts always come from the same
return. Uniqueness and identity are asserted at build time.

**Definitions.**

- *Employees* is Part I line 5, a calendar-year headcount with no hours.
  *Volunteers* is Part I line 6, the filer's own estimate.
- *Pay per employee* is Part IX lines 5-10 (officer and key-employee
  compensation, compensation of disqualified persons, other salaries and
  wages, pension contributions, other benefits, payroll taxes) divided by
  employees, kept when between $5,000 and $400,000 nominal. It is total
  people cost per head, not a wage rate; many part-time staff read as low
  pay. Medians are over organizations with a valid value; the valid counts
  are in `output/`.
- *Reported line 1e government grants share* is Part VIII line 1e over
  total revenue. Line 1e is grants only; government payments booked as
  program-service revenue (contracts, Medicaid and other reimbursements, on
  line 2) are not included. No figure here measures total government
  revenue. A blank line 1e is treated as zero (see caveat 8).
- *Expenses exceed revenue* is Part I total expenses greater than total
  revenue in the year, including non-operating items.
- *Net assets in months of expenses* is year-end total net assets divided by
  annual expenses, times twelve. Net assets include restricted funds and
  fixed assets such as buildings, so this is an accounting ratio, not months
  of cash or operating reserve, and is not comparable with the survey
  figures on cash on hand.
- Dollars are CPI-U adjusted to 2023 unless stated.

### Limitations and caveats

1. **Filing lag.** The financial and workforce series end at tax year 2023,
   filed during 2024 and 2025. They describe the sector going into 2024 and
   say nothing after that. The survey work in `docs/` covers late 2024 and
   2025. Only the BMF-based counts (density, formation, attrition,
   foundations, zip codes) are current to 2026; the spending and employee
   rows in finding 1 are TY2023.
2. **TY2023 is incomplete in this release.** Filer counts fall from 2022 to
   2023 everywhere (Davidson -3.3%, metro -1.9%, outside the 20 metros
   -5.1%). That decline mixes missing returns with exits and switches, so it
   is not a completeness rate. Every 2019-2023 ranking is shown with its
   2019-2022 version; where they differ, both are stated.
3. **Full Form 990 only.** The 990-EZ (gross receipts under $200,000 and
   assets under $500,000) has no employee count, no compensation breakdown
   and no line 1e, and the 990-N has no financials. The financial tables
   cover a minority of organizations but most of the money. Pre-2021 years
   cover only organizations that e-filed voluntarily.
4. **Leaving the full-990 panel** can mean closure, merger, falling under
   the 990-EZ threshold, or late filing. The exit cohort has not been traced
   into the 990-EZ data. The exit comparison in finding 5 is descriptive
   evidence about retained full-990 records only.
5. **Current address and classification applied to history.** The BMF
   carries one address, subsection and NTEE code per organization. Movers
   and reclassifications are not recoverable. Ruling date is the date of
   exemption recognition, not founding.
6. **BMF first-observed year steps at vintage years** (none in 2017 or
   2021; 14,461 Tennessee organizations first observed in 1989). It is not
   a formation series. Where formation is discussed, ruling year is used.
7. **BMF asset sums by zip code** come from each organization's latest
   return, are missing for 990-N filers, and are dominated by whichever large
   institutions have a mailing address in the zip. They locate large balance
   sheets, not neighborhood resources or need.
8. **Blank line 1e treated as zero.** Line 1e is blank for 63% of Davidson
   full-990 filers in 2023 and 63% outside the 20 metros. The Phase 0
   extraction leaves the amount empty when the XML element is absent, which
   is how a filer with nothing on the line files, but this has not been
   verified against source filings. Blank shares are similar across the
   comparison groups, so comparisons are less exposed than levels.
9. **Volunteer counts** are self-reported estimates, blank for about one in
   five Davidson filers, and swing with a few organizations (Second Harvest
   reports 25,000; two organizations account for half of Davidson's
   2019-2023 decline).
10. **QCEW is not on the same basis.** QCEW reports wages per annual-average
    job for an industry in a county; the nonprofit measure is compensation
    including benefits per calendar-year head for an NTEE subsector. The
    two are shown side by side, not equated.

## Findings

### 1. Population moved to the collar counties; nonprofit capacity did not

Davidson's share of the metro's registered nonprofits has fallen from 47% in
2000 to 42% in 2026 as the collar grew, but spending and jobs remain in
Davidson and, to a lesser degree, Williamson.

Registered 501(c)(3) organizations (including private foundations) per
10,000 residents, from the current BMF with activity windows applied:

| County | Pop. 2023 | Pop. growth 2010-23 | Orgs/10k 2010 | Orgs/10k 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 712,334 | 13% | 49.4 | 58.2 |
| Williamson | 264,460 | 44% | 56.5 | 62.6 |
| Rutherford | 367,101 | 39% | 24.1 | 29.2 |
| Sumner | 207,994 | 29% | 26.9 | 34.5 |
| Wilson | 163,674 | 43% | 28.6 | 34.6 |
| Maury | 110,760 | 36% | 33.0 | 38.4 |

Full-990 charity spending and jobs per resident, TY2023 (caveats 1, 3, 5):

| County | Charity filers | Expenses per resident | Charity employees per 1,000 | Human services expenses per resident | Human services employees per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 883 | $6,546 | 67.1 | $1,564 | 21.0 |
| Williamson | 331 | $2,994 | 25.7 | $992 | 9.1 |
| Rutherford | 145 | $1,008 | 17.1 | $272 | 2.6 |
| Wilson | 74 | $840 | 7.6 | $104 | 1.3 |
| Sumner | 115 | $441 | 5.1 | $195 | 2.2 |
| Maury | 57 | $1,070 | 12.5 | $176 | 2.9 |

Rutherford is the metro's second most populous county and has grown 39%
since 2010, yet hosts 37 human-services charities filing a full 990 with
2.6 employees per 1,000 residents, against 21 in Davidson. Williamson is
the exception. Every county's organization density rose between 2010 and
2023, so the collar is catching up in counts, not in capacity. Whether that
is a service gap depends on how far Davidson organizations reach, which
these data cannot show.

### 2. Inside Davidson, recently recognized charities cluster in a few zip codes

Among charities active in 2026, ranked by the number recognized by the IRS
since 2020 (current address; caveats 5 and 7):

| Zip | Area | Charities | Recognized 2020+ | Of which human services | Organizations with assets over $10M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 37013 | Antioch | 273 | 130 | 40 | 2 |
| 37211 | South Nashville | 282 | 115 | 34 | 8 |
| 37203 | Midtown | 337 | 102 | 30 | 32 |
| 37209 | West Nashville | 244 | 86 | 30 | 10 |
| 37215 | Green Hills | 233 | 81 | 23 | 9 |
| 37207 | North Nashville | 177 | 75 | 32 | 2 |

Antioch and South Nashville lead on recent recognitions and have few
organizations with large balance sheets; Midtown is third on recent
recognitions and holds the most large institutions. So recent formation is
not simply "away from the institutions". The narrower statement that holds
is that the two zips with the most recently recognized charities, and
North Nashville, have two large organizations each. Full table in
`output/explore-8-bmf.txt`.

### 3. Formation, attrition, and foundations (BMF, current)

- Nashville's stock of 501(c)(3)s grew 29% from 2019 to 2026, sixth of 20
  metros (Austin 37%, Atlanta and Raleigh 33%). Attrition is close to
  peers: 21% of organizations active in 2019 were gone by 2026 (peer
  median 20%).
- Among charities recognized since 2020, religion is 16% of Nashville's
  against 13% in peers, arts 8.6% against 7.3%, human services 35% against
  38%.
- Private foundations are growing fastest in the collar. Williamson has 7.3
  per 10,000 residents against Davidson's 5.7, and its count grew 48% since
  2015 against Davidson's 23%. The largest remain in Davidson (Dettwiller
  $251M, Scarlett $249M, Frist $196M, HCA Healthcare $193M, Living Legacy
  $165M).
- Most registered organizations are small: among those with a reported
  revenue figure, 60% in Davidson and 58% to 84% in the collar counties
  report under $50,000; roughly three in ten have no revenue figure at all
  (990-N filers and non-filers).

### 4. Funding: human services charities report less in government grants than elsewhere

Reported line 1e government grants as a share of revenue, 2023, charities
excluding hospitals and universities (caveats 1, 8; not total government
revenue):

| | Reporting any line 1e amount | Line 1e / revenue | Human services: line 1e / revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 34% | 14.8% | 15.7% (13th of 20 peer counties) |
| Nashville metro | 30% | 12.7% | 13.2% |
| Peer metros combined | 29% | 18.5% | 21.8% |
| Rest of US | 33% | 14.8% | 23.8% |

Davidson's overall line 1e share matches the rest of the US. The difference
is in human services, where Davidson's charities report 16 cents of revenue
on line 1e against 22 cents in the peer metros and 24 cents nationally;
among the 20 peer counties Davidson is 13th, in the lower half but not an
outlier (Austin 49%, Richmond 3.5%). The collar pulls the metro figure down:
human services charities in Williamson report 1.4% and in Rutherford 3.1%
(all charities: 3.6% and 4.9%), and the 13 collar counties together report
7.8%. Davidson's share has fallen each year since 2020 (17.0% to 14.8%).

The median Davidson charity draws 77% of revenue from contributions and
grants of all kinds (Rest of US 69%). The largest line 1e amounts are
charter school networks (KIPP, LEAD, Valor, RePublic, STEM Prep, each
reporting 84 to 96% of revenue on line 1e), the Tennessee Performing Arts
Center, the Mid-Cumberland community action and human resource agencies,
and Second Harvest.

### 5. Workforce: more organizations, more spending, no more jobs, higher pay per head

Charities excluding hospitals and universities, real 2023 dollars (caveats
1-4). The 2019-2022 column shows the sensitivity to the incomplete TY2023.

| | Filers 2019-23 | Employees 2019-23 | Employees 2019-22 | Real expenses 2019-23 | Median real pay per head 2019-23 | Same, 2019-22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | +16% | -5.9% | -1.0% | +5% | +6.9% (1st of 20 counties) | +3.6% (6th of 20) |
| Nashville metro | +26% | -4.4% | -0.1% | +7% | +9.9% (1st of 20 metros) | +7.2% (1st of 20) |
| Peer metros combined | +21% | +19% | +9% | -1% | +0.8% | -0.5% |
| Rest of US | +16% | -1.9% | +9% | +2% | +0.4% | +0.3% |

Employees in this release are lower in 2023 than in 2019 in both Davidson
and the metro, but through 2022 they were flat, so the fall is partly a
TY2023 coverage effect and should be described as observed in this release,
not as an established decline. The metro's pay-per-head rise leads the 20
metros under either endpoint. Davidson's leads the 20 counties through 2023
but is sixth through 2022 (Cincinnati leads at +5.5%), so the county
ranking is not robust. Davidson's median pay per head in 2023 was $46,848,
fifth highest among the 20 counties (Atlanta $54,453, Denver $53,436,
Austin $52,809, Indianapolis $47,636).

Human services pay per head in the metro rose from $36,400 to $41,700
(+14.7%). For context only (caveat 10): BLS private social-assistance pay
per job in Davidson rose from $36,900 to $41,500 in 2023 dollars (+12.5%),
and all private pay rose 6.3%. The two measures are not the same thing and
this does not show that nonprofits kept pace with the private market.

Part of the rise is composition. Among organizations present in both 2019
and 2023, the metro's median within-organization real pay change was +4.1%
(peer metros +3.2%, Rest of US +3.5%). Organizations with staff in 2019
that no longer filed a full 990 by 2023 had paid less per head in 2019
than those that stayed. In the metro the median gap is $9,900 (113 leavers
with a valid value against 734 stayers; bootstrap 95% interval -$15,200 to
-$5,200). In Davidson the gap is $4,600 (70 against 429; interval -$15,600
to +$3,500, so not distinguishable from zero). In the peer metros and the
rest of the US the gap is within a few hundred dollars of zero. Caveat 4
applies: this says nothing about whether the leavers closed.

Human services charities present in both years went from 34% to 43% with
expenses exceeding revenue (peer metros 39% to 45%, Rest of US 40% to 44%),
while their median net assets rose from 9.6 to 10.8 months of expenses.
Across all Davidson charities in 2023, 40% had expenses exceeding revenue
and 20% held net assets under three months of expenses, both at the
national level.

### 6. Volunteers: more volunteers per paid employee than the national norm, and a declining reported total

2023, charities excluding hospitals and universities (caveat 9):

| | Reporting a positive volunteer count | Reporting any value (including zero) | Median volunteers, positive reporters with staff | Median volunteers per employee | Human services: volunteers per employee |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 66% | 81% | 50 | 4.0 | 5.1 |
| Nashville collar | 55% | 67% | 38 | 5.0 | |
| Peer metros combined | 62% | 75% | | 4.1 | |
| Rest of US | 59% | 73% | | 2.6 | 2.5 |

Davidson's human services charities report twice the volunteers per paid
employee of their national counterparts; among the 20 peer counties
Davidson's 4.0 overall sits in the middle (Charlotte 5.9, St. Louis 2.8).
The reported Davidson total fell from 226,840 in 2019 to 173,719 in 2023
(-23%); Hands On Nashville and the Tennessee Environmental Council account
for 26,000 of the 53,000 decline. Among the 377 organizations with a
positive count in both years, the total fell 22% but the median change was
zero: 46% reported fewer, 37% more. In human services 52% reported fewer,
median -7%. Nationally 43% reported fewer. These are estimates from the
retained returns, not a measured change in distinct volunteers or hours.

## What this could become

- A county capacity map for Metro and the Community Foundation (finding 1,
  with the service-area caveat explicit; the density layer is current, the
  spending layer is TY2023), and a zip-level view of recent recognitions
  (finding 2).
- A funding-mix note on human services (finding 4), new relative to the
  survey work, with line 1e named for what it is. The TY2024 Phase 0 file
  (partial, early filers) could extend it by a year; no TY2024 result exists
  yet.
- The pay and exit pattern (finding 5) needs the exit cohort traced into
  the 990-EZ before it is cited anywhere.

## Reproducibility

`run-all.R` rebuilds everything: `build-panel.R` (BMF universe and the
national panel), `build-external.R` (Census, QCEW and Phase 0 downloads with
sha256 checks), `build-peers.R`, then `explore-1` through `explore-10`,
writing console output to `output/`. Every read is pinned in `_pins.csv`
with a vintage and, for files, a sha256. The BMF is read from a rolling
URL; its manifest vintage and sha256 are recorded so the build can be
identified but not re-fetched once the master rolls. The e-file CSVs
(about 6 GB, 24 files) are those synced for
`requests/2026-06-milwaukee-msa`, identified by sha256 in that folder's
`_efile_inputs.csv`. The folder is therefore reproducible from its inputs
as identified, not from the folder alone.
